results.question: Do creatures phasing back in trigger enter the battlefield abilities?
results.text: No, creatures phasing back in do not trigger enter-the-battlefield abilities. Phasing in does not cause a permanent to change zones; it is treated as though it exists on the battlefield again, but it never left the battlefield. Rule [702.26d] explicitly states that zone-change triggers don't trigger when a permanent phases in or out, and that effects checking a phased-in permanent's history won't treat the phasing event as having caused the permanent to leave or enter the battlefield. Since enter-the-battlefield abilities are zone-change triggers (as defined in [603.6a] and [603.6c]), they do not trigger upon phasing in.

results.question: how does trample work with deathtouch?
results.text: When a creature with both trample and deathtouch attacks and is blocked, the deathtouch ability dramatically reduces how much damage must be assigned to each blocking creature before excess damage can trample over to the defending player or planeswalker. Under the trample rules, the attacking creature's controller must assign "lethal damage" to all blocking creatures before any damage can be assigned to the player or planeswalker being attacked [702.19b]. Deathtouch modifies what counts as lethal damage: any nonzero amount of combat damage assigned to a creature by a source with deathtouch is considered lethal damage [702.2c]. This means the attacking creature's controller only needs to assign 1 damage to each blocking creature (regardless of that creature's toughness) to satisfy the lethal-damage requirement, and all remaining damage can be assigned as excess damage to the defending player or planeswalker. This interaction is also reflected in the excess-damage rules, which state that any amount of damage greater than 1 is excess damage if the source dealing that damage to a creature has deathtouch [120.4a]. Note that the deathtouch-based destruction of the blocking creatures will occur later as a state-based action after the damage is dealt [704.5h], but it does not affect the damage assignment step itself.

results.question: is storm a triggered ability that can be countered?
results.text: Yes, storm is a triggered ability, and it can be countered by effects that specifically counter abilities. Storm is defined as a triggered ability that functions on the stack [702.40a]. Because it is a triggered ability, it is not a spell [113.9]. While it is on the stack, it can be countered by effects that counter abilities, but not by effects that counter only spells [113.9].

results.question: can i use cards with hybrid mana symbols in a commander deck that only has one of those colors?
results.text: Yes, you can include a card with a hybrid mana symbol in a Commander deck even if your commander's color identity contains only one of the two colors in that hybrid symbol. A hybrid mana symbol is all of its component colors [107.4e], so a card with a hybrid mana symbol has a color identity that includes both colors [903.4f]. For example, a card with a {R/G} hybrid symbol has a color identity of both red and green. If your commander's color identity is only red, the card's green color identity would fall outside the commander's color identity, making the card illegal under rule 903.5c. However, if your commander's color identity is red and green (like Wort, the Raidmother), the card is legal because both colors in its color identity are found in the commander's color identity. The key point is that a hybrid symbol contributes both colors to the card's color identity, not just one, so the commander must have both colors in their color identity for the card to be legal. If your commander has only one of the two colors, the card is not allowed.

results.question: can I respond to the untap step?
results.text: No, you cannot respond to the untap step. No player receives priority during the untap step, so no spells can be cast or resolve and no abilities can be activated or resolve [502.4]. The untap step consists entirely of turn-based actions that don't use the stack (phasing, day/night check, and untapping) and ends when those actions are completed [500.3]. The first time a player gets priority after the untap step is during the upkeep step, after any abilities that triggered during the untap step or at the beginning of upkeep are put onto the stack [503.1a].

results.question: are creatures still considered attacking creatures during the end of combat step?
results.text: Yes, creatures are still considered attacking creatures during the end of combat step. A creature remains an attacking creature until it is removed from combat or the combat phase ends, whichever comes first. The end of combat step is the fifth and final step of the combat phase, so the combat phase has not yet ended during that step. Therefore, creatures that were declared as attackers (or put onto the battlefield attacking) earlier in the combat phase are still attacking creatures during the end of combat step. They stop being attacking creatures only after the end of combat step ends, at which point all creatures are removed from combat and the combat phase is over.

results.question: Do you cast lands?
results.text: No, you do not cast lands. Lands are not spells and are never cast. Instead, playing a land is a special action that puts the land directly onto the battlefield without using the stack. This applies to all land cards, including artifact lands, which can only be played as lands and cannot be cast as spells. The action of playing a land does not involve paying a mana cost, and lands have no mana cost (which represents an unpayable cost).

results.question: can I sacrifice an evoked creature before that creature's evoke triggered ability resolves?
results.text:
Yes, you can sacrifice an evoked creature before its evoke triggered ability resolves, provided you have priority and a way to sacrifice it. The evoke triggered ability uses the stack and can be responded to like any other triggered ability. When the evoked creature enters the battlefield, the evoke triggered ability ("When this permanent enters, if its evoke cost was paid, its controller sacrifices it") triggers and goes on the stack. Before that ability resolves, each player gets priority and can cast spells or activate abilities, including those that sacrifice the creature. If you sacrifice the evoked creature in response, the evoke triggered ability will still resolve, but when it does, the creature is no longer on the battlefield to be sacrificed, so the sacrifice instruction does nothing (you can't sacrifice a permanent you no longer control).

This assumes you have a spell or ability that lets you sacrifice the creature at instant speed while the evoke trigger is on the stack. The evoke triggered ability itself does not give you a window to sacrifice the creature before it resolves — it simply instructs you to sacrifice the creature when it resolves. The window to sacrifice the creature before that happens comes from the normal priority system: after the evoke trigger is put on the stack, players get priority and can respond.

If the question is whether you can sacrifice the creature *as a cost* to pay for the evoke triggered ability itself, the answer is no — the evoke triggered ability does not have a cost of sacrificing a creature; it simply instructs you to sacrifice the creature as part of its effect when it resolves. You cannot pre-pay that sacrifice to satisfy the ability early, because costs are paid when spells or abilities are cast or activated, not during resolution of a triggered ability that merely instructs a sacrifice (see rule 118.10).

results.question: if a card loses all abilities, does that include keyword abilities?
results.text: Yes. When a card loses all abilities, that includes keyword abilities. Keyword abilities are a subset of abilities — they are simply abilities that are common enough to be represented by a single word or phrase instead of being spelled out in full rules text [702.1]. An effect that says an object “loses all abilities” removes every ability the object has, including any keyword abilities, because it removes all instances of each ability [113.10b]. There is no distinction in the rules between “regular” abilities and keyword abilities for purposes of ability removal; both are abilities and both are removed.

results.question: can i draw cards if i'm already at my maximum hand size?
results.text: Yes, you can draw cards even if you are already at your maximum hand size. There is no rule that prevents a player from drawing cards simply because their hand size equals or exceeds their maximum. The maximum hand size only matters during the cleanup step, when the active player must discard down to that number (rule 514.1, rule 703.4n). Outside of that specific turn-based action, you may hold any number of cards in your hand (rule 402.2). Drawing cards is handled by the normal draw rules (rule 121.2), and nothing in those rules checks your current hand size against your maximum before allowing a draw. If you draw while at or above your maximum, you will simply have more cards than your maximum until your next cleanup step, at which point you must discard the excess.

results.question: what happens when a planeswalker has 0 or less loyalty counters?
results.text: When a planeswalker on the battlefield has zero loyalty counters, it is put into its owner's graveyard as a state-based action. This happens automatically the next time a player would receive priority, without using the stack. The rules do not describe a case where a planeswalker has less than zero loyalty counters; loyalty is simply the number of loyalty counters on it, and that number cannot be negative. If damage or a cost would remove more counters than the planeswalker currently has, all of its counters are removed, leaving it at zero loyalty, and the state-based action then sends it to the graveyard.

results.question: do non-creature artifacts die?
results.text: No. Only a creature or planeswalker can “die.” The term “dies” is defined as “is put into a graveyard from the battlefield” and applies exclusively to creatures and planeswalkers. A noncreature artifact that is put into a graveyard from the battlefield is not a creature or planeswalker, so it does not “die” — it simply moves to the graveyard.

results.question: what happens if i should draw a card when my library is empty?
results.text: You lose the game the next time state-based actions are checked. The attempt to draw from an empty library is a state-based action that causes you to lose under rule 704.5b, and this is also covered by rules 121.4 and 104.3c. The loss doesn't happen immediately in the middle of a spell or ability resolving; it waits until a player would receive priority, at which point state-based actions are checked and you lose.

results.question: what are the steps in combat and when do I have priority as the defending player?
results.text:
The combat phase has five steps in order: beginning of combat, declare attackers, declare blockers, combat damage, and end of combat. As the defending player, you get priority during each of those steps after any turn-based actions for that step are completed and any triggered abilities that go on the stack have been put there. Specifically:

- **Beginning of combat step**: The turn-based action (choosing a defending player in applicable multiplayer games) happens immediately after the step begins [703.4h]. After that, the active player gets priority first, then you (the nonactive player) get priority when the active player passes [117.1].
- **Declare attackers step**: The active player declares attackers as a turn-based action immediately after the step begins. After that, the active player gets priority, then you get priority when the active player passes.
- **Declare blockers step**: You declare blockers as a turn-based action immediately after the step begins [703.4j, 509.1]. After that, the active player gets priority, then you get priority when the active player passes.
- **Combat damage step**: Combat damage is assigned and then dealt simultaneously as turn-based actions immediately after the step begins [703.4k, 510.1, 510.2]. After that, the active player gets priority, then you get priority when the active player passes. (If any attacking or blocking creature has first strike or double strike, there are two combat damage steps, and priority works the same way in each.)
- **End of combat step**: This step has no turn-based actions [511.1]. The active player gets priority first, then you get priority when the active player passes.

In a two-player game, you are automatically the defending player [506.2]. In a multiplayer game, whether you are a defending player depends on the variant and options used; if the active player’s opponents don’t all automatically become defending players, the active player chooses one opponent as the defending player during the beginning of combat step [506.2a, 507.1]. If you are not chosen, you are not a defending player and your creatures cannot block attackers directed at the chosen defending player (unless a card effect says otherwise). The priority timing within each step remains the same regardless of how many defending players there are.

results.question: can i respond to a mana ability?
results.text: No, you cannot respond to a mana ability. Mana abilities do not use the stack, so they resolve immediately and cannot be targeted, countered, or otherwise responded to.

results.question: can I respond to a cost being paid?
results.text: No, you cannot respond to a cost being paid. Paying a cost is the action of carrying out the instructions specified by a spell, ability, or effect, and it does not use the stack. Once a player begins to pay a cost, that payment happens immediately and cannot be responded to. Only after the cost is fully paid and the spell or ability that required it is on the stack (or, for special actions, after the action is complete) do players receive priority and have a chance to respond.

results.question: can you explain layers?
results.text: Yes. Layers are the system Magic uses to determine the order in which continuous effects are applied to an object’s characteristics. The game starts with the object’s printed values (or the values defined for a token or copy), then applies effects in a fixed sequence of layers: Layer 1 (copiable values), Layer 2 (control-changing), Layer 3 (text-changing), Layer 4 (type-changing), Layer 5 (color-changing), Layer 6 (ability-adding/removing), and Layer 7 (power/toughness). Within each layer or sublayer, effects are normally applied in timestamp order (earliest first), unless a dependency exists, which overrides timestamp order. If a single effect has parts that apply in different layers, each part is applied in its appropriate layer, and the effect continues to apply to the same set of objects in every layer even if the source of the effect is removed mid-process. The application is continuous and automatic, so any change to an object’s characteristics is instantaneous. For example, if a 2/2 creature gets a +1/+1 counter (Layer 7c), then a spell gives it +4/+4 (Layer 7c), then an enchantment gives it +0/+2 (Layer 7c), and finally an effect sets it to 0/1 (Layer 7b), the result is a 5/8 (0/1 base, plus the three Layer 7c bonuses).

results.question: how does the legend rule work?
results.text: The legend rule is a state-based action: if a single player controls two or more legendary permanents with the exact same name, that player must choose one of them to keep, and all the others are put into their owners' graveyards. This happens immediately whenever the condition is met, before any player receives priority. The rule applies only to legendary permanents controlled by the same player—legendary permanents with different names, or legendary permanents with the same name controlled by different players, are unaffected. Legendary instants and sorceries are not permanents and are not subject to this rule; instead, they have a casting restriction that requires you to control a legendary creature or planeswalker to cast them.

results.question: when does my creature die after its been marked with a lethal amount of damage?
results.text:
Your creature dies the next time state-based actions are checked after lethal damage is marked on it. State-based actions are checked right before any player would receive priority, so the creature is destroyed at that moment — not during the damage event itself.

Here’s how it works step by step. When a source without wither or infect deals damage to a creature, that much damage is marked on the creature [120.3e]. The damage itself doesn’t destroy the creature [120.5]. Instead, the game rules check state-based actions automatically whenever a player would get priority [117.5, 704.1]. If the creature has toughness greater than 0 and the total damage marked on it is greater than or equal to its toughness, the state-based action in rule 704.5g destroys it. (If the damage source had deathtouch, rule 704.5h would also destroy it, and any amount of damage from a deathtouch source counts as lethal for that check [702.2b].)

In practice, this means the creature dies after the spell or ability that dealt the damage finishes resolving, or after combat damage is dealt and the combat damage step moves toward giving a player priority. The marked damage stays on the creature until the cleanup step, but the creature is usually put into the graveyard long before then — as soon as state-based actions are next checked [120.6, 514.2].

If the question is about a specific scenario (e.g., Lightning Bolt targeting a 2/2), the creature is destroyed when state-based actions are checked after Lightning Bolt resolves, before the active player gets priority again. If combat damage is involved, all combat damage is dealt simultaneously, then state-based actions are checked before any player gets priority in the combat damage step [703.4m, 117.5].

results.question: can I cast my commander from exile?
results.text: Yes, you can cast your commander from exile, provided you are legally allowed to cast it from that zone. The commander designation stays with the card no matter which zone it moves to [903.3d]. Casting a commander from exile follows the normal rules for casting spells from exile — you need permission from a rule or effect to cast it from that zone, and no rule or effect can prohibit it [601.3f]. If you are casting your commander from the command zone, the “commander tax” (an additional {2} for each previous time you’ve cast it from the command zone that game) applies [903.8]. However, if you are casting it directly from exile (for example, because it was plotted, or because it’s the exiled half of an Adventure), you are not casting it from the command zone, so the commander tax does not apply — you pay only the spell’s normal cost or whatever alternative cost the effect granting permission provides. Note that if your commander is in exile, you also have the option to return it to the command zone as a state-based action [704.6d, 903.9a], but you are not forced to do so; you can leave it in exile and cast it from there if you have a way to do so.

results.question: what happens during the cleanup step?
results.text:
During the cleanup step, the active player first discards down to their maximum hand size (normally seven) if they have more cards than that. Then, simultaneously, all damage is removed from permanents and all “until end of turn” and “this turn” effects end. Normally, no player gets priority during the cleanup step, so no spells can be cast or abilities activated. However, if any state-based actions need to be performed or any triggered abilities are waiting to be put on the stack (including those that trigger “at the beginning of the next cleanup step”), those state-based actions are performed, those triggered abilities are put on the stack, and then the active player gets priority. Once the stack is empty and all players pass in succession, another cleanup step begins. If no state-based actions or triggered abilities are waiting, the step ends without any player receiving priority, and the turn ends.

This is the normal sequence. If an effect that ends the turn (such as from a card like Time Stop) resolves during the cleanup step, a new cleanup step begins instead, and triggered abilities that triggered during that process are put on the stack during that new cleanup step, after which the active player gets priority and another cleanup step follows. The specific rules governing this are [514.1], [514.2], [514.3]/[514.3a], [703.4n], [703.4p], [724.1d], and [724.1f].

results.question: when are state-based actions checked?
results.text: State-based actions are checked each time a player would receive priority, and also during the cleanup step. Specifically, the game checks for state-based actions right before a player would get priority (after any turn-based actions for that step or phase are handled), and then repeats the check until no more state-based actions are performed and no triggered abilities are waiting to be put on the stack. This same process also occurs during the cleanup step, with the special rule that if no state-based actions are performed on the first check and no triggered abilities are waiting, no player gets priority and the step ends. State-based actions are not checked during the resolution of a spell or ability; they only happen when the game would next give a player priority or during the cleanup step as described.

results.question: when can I concede a game?
results.text: You can concede the game at any time. Conceding doesn't use the stack, happens immediately, and causes you to leave the game and lose it right then. This right is absolute -- even if another player controls your turn, they cannot make you concede, and no card effect can override your ability to concede. In a Two-Headed Giant game, if you concede, your entire team leaves the game immediately and loses.

results.question: how do I know who the active player is?
results.text:
The active player is the player whose turn it is. In a game using the shared team turns option, the active team is the team whose turn it is, and the active player is still the player whose turn it is (the individual on that team taking the turn). A player who is being controlled by another player during their own turn remains the active player.

This is stated directly in rule 102.1: “The active player is the player whose turn it is.” Rule 805.4a adds that in shared-team-turns games, the team whose turn it is is the active team, and rule 723.3 clarifies that controlling another player doesn’t change who the active player is—the player whose turn it is stays the active player even while controlled.

In a two‑player game, the active player is simply the player currently taking the turn. In a multiplayer game with more than two players, the active player is still the player whose turn it is; the other players are nonactive players. If the game uses the shared team turns option, the active team is the team whose turn it is, and the active player is the specific player on that team who is taking the turn.

results.question: when someone other than the active player casts a spell, who gets priority first?
results.text: The active player gets priority first. After a nonactive player casts a spell, that nonactive player receives priority again (per rule 117.3c), but only after the active player has had a chance to act. The sequence is: the nonactive player casts the spell, then the active player gets priority, and only after the active player passes does the nonactive player who cast the spell get priority again. This is because rule 117.3c says the player who had priority when they cast a spell receives priority afterward, but rule 117.3b and the turn-structure rules (504.2, 508.2, 509.2, 507.2, 510.3, 505.6) consistently state that the active player gets priority after any spell or ability resolves or at the start of each step/phase. The general principle is that the active player always gets priority first whenever the stack is empty or after something resolves, and rule 117.3c is an exception that gives priority back to the caster only after the active player has had priority and passed. In a two-player game, this means the opponent (active player) gets priority first after you cast a spell on their turn. In a multiplayer game, the active player still gets priority first, then turn order proceeds, and the caster will get priority when their turn in the order arrives (which may be immediately after the active player if they are next in turn order, or later if other players are between).

results.question: when the active player cast a spell, who gets priority first?
results.text: The active player gets priority first after they cast a spell. This is stated directly in rule 117.3c: if a player has priority when they cast a spell, that player receives priority afterward. Since the active player must have priority to cast the spell in the first place, they are the one who receives priority immediately after the spell is put on the stack.

results.question: can I hold priority to cast more spells after I've cast one or more spells?
results.text: Yes. When you cast a spell while you have priority, you receive priority again immediately after that spell is cast [117.3c]. This means you can hold priority and cast another spell (or activate another ability) before any other player gets a chance to respond. The same is true after you take a special action [116.3]. In a Grand Melee game, you must specify which stack you are putting each new spell or ability onto [807.5b]. In a team game, your team has priority, not you individually, but you may still cast spells or activate abilities when your team has priority [805.5a]. Note that this only applies to spells you can legally cast at that time — for example, you can only cast a noninstant spell during your main phase when the stack is empty [117.1a], so you could not hold priority to cast a second sorcery after the first one is on the stack.

results.question: when are lore counters put on sagas?
results.text: Lore counters are put on Sagas as a turn-based action immediately after a player's precombat main phase begins. That player puts one lore counter on each Saga they control that has one or more chapter abilities. This action doesn't use the stack. [703.4f] [714.3c] [505.4]

results.question: what is a delayed triggered ability?
results.text: A delayed triggered ability is an ability created by a resolving spell or ability (or by a replacement effect or static ability) that instructs a player to do something later in the game rather than right now. It always contains the word “when,” “whenever,” or “at” (though that word usually doesn't start the ability), and it triggers only once the next time its trigger event occurs, unless it has a stated duration like “this turn.” [603.7, 603.7a, 603.7b, 610.2]

results.question: can non-permanent spells have abilities?
results.text: Yes, non-permanent spells can have abilities. Instants and sorceries have spell abilities, which are the instructions followed while the spell resolves [113.3a]. They can also have static abilities that function on the stack, such as those that modify how the spell is cast or what it can target [113.6]. Additionally, effects can grant abilities to non-permanent spells while they are on the stack, like “can’t be countered” [113.10]. However, activated and triggered abilities on non-permanent spells are rare and would only function while the spell is on the stack, as abilities of instants and sorceries usually function only there [113.6].

results.question: can I use a mana ability when a spell with split-second is on the stack?
results.text: Yes, you can activate mana abilities while a spell with split second is on the stack. Split second explicitly allows players to activate mana abilities and take special actions, even though it prevents casting other spells or activating non-mana abilities. Mana abilities themselves don't use the stack and can be activated at times when you normally couldn't take other actions, including while a split-second spell is on the stack.

results.question: [Counterspell] is on top of the stack targeting my [Divination]. When everyone passes priority, what resolves first, and does Divination still resolve?
results.text: Counterspell resolves first. When Counterspell resolves, it counters Divination, removing Divination from the stack. Divination does not resolve and none of its effects occur.

results.question: My [Charging Rhino] has trample and is blocked by [Vampire Nighthawk], which has deathtouch. How much combat damage do I have to assign to the blocker before I can trample the rest over to the player?
results.text: You must assign exactly 1 damage to Vampire Nighthawk before you can assign the remaining 3 damage to the defending player. Because Vampire Nighthawk has deathtouch, any nonzero amount of combat damage assigned to it by Charging Rhino is considered lethal damage for trample purposes [702.2c]. Charging Rhino has 4 power, so after assigning 1 damage to Vampire Nighthawk, the remaining 3 damage is excess and can be assigned to the defending player via trample [702.19b].

results.question: I have [Monastery Swiftspear] on the battlefield and I cast [Shardless Agent]. When its cascade ability puts a noncreature spell onto the stack, does Monastery Swiftspear's prowess trigger before or after that cascaded spell resolves?
results.text:
Monastery Swiftspear's prowess will trigger when you cast the noncreature spell off cascade, and that prowess trigger will resolve before the cascaded spell resolves.

Here's the sequence: You cast Shardless Agent. Shardless Agent's cascade ability triggers and goes on the stack above Shardless Agent. Cascade resolves, and you exile cards until you hit a nonland card with lesser mana value. If you choose to cast that card, you do so during the resolution of the cascade ability. Casting that noncreature spell causes Monastery Swiftspear's prowess to trigger. Because cascade is still resolving, the prowess trigger waits. Once cascade finishes resolving, the prowess trigger is put onto the stack on top of the cascaded spell (and on top of Shardless Agent). Then, when all players pass, the prowess trigger resolves, giving Monastery Swiftspear +1/+1. After that, the cascaded spell resolves, and finally Shardless Agent resolves.

This follows from the general rule that an ability that triggers when a player casts a spell resolves before that spell [Monastery Swiftspear ruling #0], and specifically that prowess goes on the stack on top of the spell that caused it to trigger and resolves before that spell [Monastery Swiftspear ruling #2]. The cascade ruling confirms that cascade triggers when you cast the spell and resolves before that spell, and that if you cast the exiled card, it goes on the stack above the spell with cascade [Shardless Agent ruling #1]. The prowess trigger then goes on top of that cascaded spell.

results.question: My opponent's [Grizzly Bears] has 2 damage marked on it. Do state-based actions make it die before my [Lightning Bolt] resolves?
results.text: No. State‑based actions are not checked during the resolution of a spell or ability. Lightning Bolt will finish resolving and deal its 3 damage to Grizzly Bears before state‑based actions are checked. After Lightning Bolt has resolved, state‑based actions see a Grizzly Bears with 5 total damage marked on it (2 existing plus 3 new) and a toughness of 2, so Grizzly Bears will be destroyed at that point.

results.question: It's my upkeep. My [Phyrexian Arena]'s beginning-of-upkeep trigger and my opponent's own beginning-of-upkeep trigger both want to go on the stack. Who chooses the order, and when exactly do they trigger?
results.text:
Both Phyrexian Arena triggers go on the stack during your upkeep, before you (the active player) get priority. You choose the relative order of the two triggers. They trigger simultaneously at the moment your upkeep step begins, but they are put on the stack in APNAP order: you, as the active player, put your triggered abilities on the stack first in any order you choose, then your opponent (the nonactive player) puts theirs on top in any order they choose. Since each player controls only one Phyrexian Arena trigger here, the result is that your opponent's trigger ends up on top of the stack and will resolve first, unless you have other triggered abilities you control that you choose to place above or below your Phyrexian Arena trigger.

Here's the step-by-step reasoning:
- When your upkeep step begins, any abilities that trigger "at the beginning of" the upkeep trigger automatically [500.6, 603.2b]. Both Phyrexian Arenas trigger at this exact moment.
- The upkeep step has no turn-based actions, so we skip straight to putting triggered abilities on the stack [503.1a, 703.3].
- Multiple triggered abilities are put on the stack in a two-part APNAP process [603.3b]. First, the active player (you) puts each triggered ability they control with a trigger condition that isn't another ability triggering on the stack in any order they choose. You control one such ability: your Phyrexian Arena trigger. You put it on the stack. Second, the nonactive player (your opponent) puts all remaining triggered abilities they control on the stack in any order they choose. They control one: their Phyrexian Arena trigger. They put it on the stack, on top of yours.
- After all triggers are on the stack and state-based actions are checked, you (the active player) receive priority [117.3a, 503.1a].
- The choice of whether to draw and lose life (the "may"-like effect is actually mandatory here, but the principle is the same) is made when each ability resolves, not when it's put on the stack [603.5].

This answer assumes a two-player game. In a multiplayer game with more than two players, the same APNAP order applies: the active player puts their triggers on the stack first, then each nonactive player in turn order puts theirs on top. The triggers still all go on the stack during the active player's upkeep before that player gets priority.

results.question: I cast a sorcery with buyback and pay its buyback cost, then copy that spell with [Fork]. Once everything resolves, how many copies of the card end up back in my hand?
results.text: You get exactly one copy of the card back in your hand: the original sorcery card returns to your hand from the stack because you paid its buyback cost. The copy created by Fork is not a card and goes to the graveyard (and then ceases to exist) when it resolves; it cannot return to your hand.

results.question: I have a face-down manifested card that's really [Lightning Bolt]. It dies and I imprint it on [Mimic Vat]. Later I activate Mimic Vat's copy ability -- do I get a token?
results.text: No, you do not get a token. The manifested card is Lightning Bolt, an instant card. Mimic Vat's second ability tries to create a token that's a copy of the exiled card, but the exiled card is a nonpermanent card (an instant). According to Mimic Vat ruling #0, you cannot create a token that's a copy of a nonpermanent card, so no token is created.

results.question: My [Fiend Hunter]'s enters-the-battlefield ability is on the stack, about to exile a creature. I copy that ability with [Lithoform Engine] and target a second creature. Both get exiled. When Fiend Hunter later leaves the battlefield, do both come back?
results.text: Yes, both exiled creatures return to the battlefield. Fiend Hunter's two abilities are linked: the second ability refers to cards exiled by the first. When you copy the first ability with Lithoform Engine, the copy is also linked to that same second ability, so the second ability sees all cards exiled by the original and the copy. When Fiend Hunter leaves the battlefield, its second ability returns both exiled creatures to the battlefield under their owners' control.

results.question: My own [Banishing Light] has an opponent's creature exiled. On my opponent's turn I cast [Teferi's Protection], phasing out my Banishing Light. Does the exiled creature return to the battlefield?
results.text: No, the exiled creature does not return to the battlefield. When Banishing Light phases out, it does not leave the battlefield, so its “until this enchantment leaves the battlefield” condition is not met. The one-shot effect that would return the exiled creature is not created, and the creature remains in exile. This is directly confirmed by Teferi's Protection ruling #21, which states that one-shot effects waiting “until [this] leaves the battlefield” won’t happen when a permanent phases out. Phasing out is not leaving the battlefield (rule 702.26d), so Banishing Light’s exile duration continues indefinitely while Banishing Light is phased out. If Banishing Light later phases in and then leaves the battlefield, the return effect would trigger at that point.

results.question: I cast [Emrakul, the Promised End]. In response to its cast trigger, my opponent tries to [Counterspell] it. Can they even target it given protection from instants, and if it's countered, do I still control their next turn?
results.text:
Yes, your opponent can target Emrakul, the Promised End with Counterspell while Emrakul, the Promised End is on the stack, and if Counterspell resolves and counters Emrakul, the Promised End, you still control their next turn.

Here's why:

1. **Targeting Emrakul, the Promised End on the stack:** Emrakul, the Promised End has "protection from instants." Protection abilities only function while the permanent with protection is on the battlefield. While Emrakul, the Promised End is a spell on the stack, it does not yet have protection from instants, so it can be targeted by instant spells like Counterspell. This is explicitly stated in Emrakul, the Promised End's rulings: "Protection abilities only apply while the object with the ability is on the battlefield. Notably, Emrakul may be the target of a spell that targets it while on the stack, such as Syncopate." [Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #2]

2. **The cast trigger still resolves:** Emrakul, the Promised End's triggered ability ("When you cast this spell, you gain control of target opponent during that player's next turn...") triggers when you cast Emrakul, the Promised End and goes on the stack above Emrakul, the Promised End. This triggered ability exists independently of the Emrakul, the Promised End spell. Even if Counterspell counters Emrakul, the Promised End, the triggered ability is already on the stack and will resolve normally (assuming its target is still legal), giving you control of the opponent's next turn. The triggered ability is not a spell and is not countered by Counterspell, which only counters spells. [113.9] [603.1a] [608.2b]

3. **Order of events:** Assuming the opponent casts Counterspell in response to the cast trigger (the most common scenario), the stack looks like this (top to bottom): Counterspell, Emrakul's cast trigger, Emrakul spell. Counterspell resolves first, countering Emrakul. Then the cast trigger resolves, giving you control of the opponent's next turn. If the opponent instead cast Counterspell targeting Emrakul before the cast trigger was put on the stack (which isn't possible, as the trigger goes on the stack immediately after casting), the outcome would be the same: the trigger still exists and resolves.

results.question: My cascade spell exiles cards until it hits [Valki, God of Lies], whose back face is the seven-mana planeswalker Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor. Is that a legal cascade hit, and can I cast the Tibalt side for free?
results.text:
Yes, Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor is a legal cascade hit, and you may cast the Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor side for free.

Here's why. Cascade (rule 702.85a) exiles cards until you hit a nonland card whose mana value is less than the cascading spell's mana value. For a modal double-faced card (MDFC) like Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor, you consider only the characteristics of the face you intend to play when determining legality (Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor ruling #14). The front face, Valki, God of Lies, has mana value 2. If the cascading spell's mana value is greater than 2, Valki, God of Lies qualifies as a legal hit because its front face's mana value is less than the cascading spell's mana value.

Once the card is exiled and cascade allows you to cast it, you may cast either face that fits the criteria of the effect (Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor ruling #16). Cascade says you may cast the exiled card without paying its mana cost if the resulting spell's mana value is less than the cascading spell's mana value. The resulting spell's mana value is determined by the face you cast. If you cast Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor, its mana value is 7 (derived from its own mana cost, {5}{B}{R}). For Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor to be cast for free, the cascading spell's mana value must be greater than 7. If the cascading spell's mana value is, say, 8 or more, you can cast Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor without paying its mana cost. If the cascading spell's mana value is 7 or less, you could still cast Valki, God of Lies for free (since its mana value is 2), but Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor would not be free because its mana value is not less than the cascading spell's mana value.

In summary: Valki, God of Lies is a legal cascade hit based on its front face's mana value of 2. You may then choose to cast Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor, and if the cascading spell's mana value is greater than 7, you cast Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor for free. If the cascading spell's mana value is 7 or less, you can still cast Valki, God of Lies for free, but Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor would not be free.
citations: Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor ruling #14
Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor ruling #16

results.question: I cast [Emrakul, the Promised End]. With its cast trigger on the stack, I copy that trigger with [Lithoform Engine]. Then I untap Lithoform Engine with [Voltaic Key] and use it again to copy [Emrakul, the Promised End] itself as a permanent spell. How many of my opponent's turns do I control, do I get a second Emrakul, and does copying the Emrakul spell give me another control-a-turn trigger?
results.text:
You will control two of your opponent's turns, you will get a second Emrakul, the Promised End token, and copying the Emrakul, the Promised End permanent spell does **not** give you another control-a-turn trigger.

Here's the breakdown:

1. **Copying the cast trigger with Lithoform Engine:** The original cast trigger of Emrakul, the Promised End is on the stack. Lithoform Engine's first ability copies that triggered ability. The copy resolves, giving you control of the targeted opponent during their next turn and setting up the delayed extra turn. Then the original cast trigger resolves, doing the same thing. You now have two separate instances of the control effect and two separate delayed extra-turn effects. Per Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #14, multiple player-controlling effects that affect the same player overwrite each other, with the last one created being the one that works. However, each ability's effect will create an extra turn. So you will control the opponent's next turn (from the last-resolved trigger) and they will get two extra turns after that, which you will also control because the control effect applies to the next turn they take (Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #16).

2. **Copying the Emrakul, the Promised End permanent spell with Lithoform Engine:** Lithoform Engine's third ability copies the Emrakul, the Promised End permanent spell on the stack. This creates a copy of the spell on the stack. Per rule 111.13, a copy of a permanent spell becomes a token as it resolves. So you will get a second Emrakul, the Promised End as a token. Per Lithoform Engine ruling #6, the copy is not cast, so abilities that trigger when you cast a spell (like Emrakul, the Promised End's own cast trigger) do not trigger. You do not get another control-a-turn trigger from the copy.

**Timing assumption:** This answer assumes you are using Lithoform Engine's abilities while the original cast trigger and the original Emrakul, the Promised End spell are both still on the stack, and that you are doing so in the order described (copy trigger, untap, copy spell). The order of resolution of the two trigger copies and the original trigger matters for which control effect "wins" (the last one to resolve), but you will still control two turns total.

results.question: I've imprinted a creature on [Mimic Vat] and activate its ability to make a token copy. While that ability is on the stack, I copy it with [Lithoform Engine]. Do I get two tokens?
results.text: Yes, you get two tokens. When the copy of Mimic Vat's activated ability created by Lithoform Engine resolves, it creates a token that is a copy of the card exiled with Mimic Vat. Then, when the original Mimic Vat ability resolves, it also creates a token that is a copy of the exiled card. Both abilities refer to the same exiled card, and nothing in the rules prevents multiple tokens from being created from the same exiled card in this way.

results.question: An opponent controls an untapped [Trinisphere], and I have a permanent that makes my green spells cost {1} less. I want to cast [Awaken the Woods] for value. If I cast it with X=0, what does it cost and what do I get, and what X should I actually choose?
results.text:
If you cast Awaken the Woods with X=0, the total cost is {G}{G} and you create zero tokens. To get value, you should choose X=1 or higher. With X=1, the total cost is {2}{G} and you create one token. With X=2, the total cost is {3}{G} and you create two tokens. With X=3 or more, the total cost is {X}{G} and you create X tokens.

Here's the step-by-step reasoning:

1. **Announcing X**: As you cast Awaken the Woods, you announce the value of X. This is part of the proposal of the spell (rule 601.2b). The mana cost of Awaken the Woods is {X}{G}{G}. The value of X is not defined by the spell's text, so you choose it (rule 107.3a).

2. **Cost reduction**: You have an effect that makes your green spells cost {1} less. This is a cost reduction. The spell's mana cost is {X}{G}{G}. The generic portion of that cost is {X}. The cost reduction reduces the generic mana required by {1}.

3. **Trinisphere's effect**: Trinisphere's effect applies after all cost increases and reductions are applied, and only if the mana component of the spell's cost is less than three mana (Trinisphere ruling #0). The mana component is the total amount of mana in the cost, not the mana value. Trinisphere adds generic mana to bring the total mana component up to three.

Let's calculate the total cost for different values of X:

- **X=0**: Mana cost is {0}{G}{G} = {G}{G}. Cost reduction of {1} applies, but the generic portion is already 0, so the reduction has no effect (rule 601.2f says the mana component can't be reduced below {0}). The cost is {G}{G}. The mana component is 2 (two green mana). Trinisphere sees the mana component is less than 3, so it increases the cost to {3} total mana. Since the original cost was {G}{G}, Trinisphere adds {1} generic mana, making the total cost {1}{G}{G}. You create X=0 tokens.

- **X=1**: Mana cost is {1}{G}{G}. Cost reduction of {1} applies, reducing the generic portion from {1} to {0}. The cost becomes {G}{G}. The mana component is 2. Trinisphere increases the cost to {3} total mana, adding {1} generic mana. Total cost is {1}{G}{G}. You create 1 token.

- **X=2**: Mana cost is {2}{G}{G}. Cost reduction of {1} applies, reducing the generic portion from {2} to {1}. The cost becomes {1}{G}{G}. The mana component is 3 (one generic, two green). Trinisphere sees the mana component is 3, so it does nothing. Total cost is {1}{G}{G}. You create 2 tokens.

- **X=3**: Mana cost is {3}{G}{G}. Cost reduction of {1} applies, reducing the generic portion from {3} to {2}. The cost becomes {2}{G}{G}. The mana component is 4. Trinisphere does nothing. Total cost is {2}{G}{G}. You create 3 tokens.

Notice that X=1 and X=2 both result in a total cost of {1}{G}{G}, but X=2 gives you two tokens instead of one. X=3 costs {2}{G}{G} and gives three tokens. So the most efficient choice is X=2, which gives you two tokens for the same cost as X=1. X=0 is the worst, costing {1}{G}{G} for zero tokens.

**Important note on Trinisphere's application**: Trinisphere's effect is applied after all cost increases and reductions, and it looks at the mana component of the total cost. The mana component is the total amount of mana in the cost, counting each colored mana symbol as 1. Trinisphere adds generic mana to make the total mana component equal to 3. It does not change the colored mana requirements. The cost reduction you have reduces the generic portion of the cost before Trinisphere applies, which can sometimes cause Trinisphere to kick in when it otherwise wouldn't (as seen with X=1).

results.question: [Grist, the Hunger Tide] is in my graveyard. Can I return it with [Animate Dead], and what happens?
results.text: Yes, you can return Grist, the Hunger Tide from your graveyard with Animate Dead. In the graveyard, Grist, the Hunger Tide is a creature card (a Legendary Planeswalker Creature — Grist Insect) [Grist, the Hunger Tide ruling #1], so it is a legal target for Animate Dead's "enchant creature card in a graveyard" ability. When Animate Dead's enters-the-battlefield trigger resolves, it returns Grist, the Hunger Tide to the battlefield under your control and attaches Animate Dead to it. Once on the battlefield, Grist, the Hunger Tide stops being a creature and is only a planeswalker [Grist, the Hunger Tide ruling #1]. Animate Dead's "Enchanted creature gets -1/-0" effect will not apply to Grist, the Hunger Tide because it is not a creature on the battlefield. Animate Dead remains attached to Grist, the Hunger Tide, and if Animate Dead leaves the battlefield, Grist, the Hunger Tide's controller must sacrifice it.

results.question: My commander [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave] has four +1/+1 counters on it. It dies, I move it to the command zone, then recast it. Does it keep the counters, and does [Doubling Season] double them as it re-enters?
results.text:
Yes, Skullbriar, the Walking Grave keeps the four +1/+1 counters when it moves to the command zone, and Doubling Season will double the number of +1/+1 counters placed on it as it re-enters the battlefield, resulting in Skullbriar entering with eight +1/+1 counters.

Here's the step-by-step reasoning:

1. **Skullbriar's ability keeps the counters in the command zone.** Skullbriar's text says, "Counters remain on Skullbriar as it moves to any zone other than a player's hand or library." This is a specific exception to the general rule that counters cease to exist when an object changes zones [122.2]. The command zone is not a hand or library, so when Skullbriar dies and you choose to put it into the command zone (via the state-based action in [903.9a]/[704.6d]), the four +1/+1 counters remain on it. Skullbriar ruling #3 confirms that counters affect its power/toughness in zones other than the battlefield, and ruling #1 confirms it retains all counters, not just +1/+1 counters.

2. **Recasting Skullbriar from the command zone.** When you cast Skullbriar from the command zone, it moves from the command zone to the stack, then to the battlefield. Skullbriar's ability applies each time it changes zones, so the counters remain on it through each of these moves (none of which are a hand or library). When it enters the battlefield, it is a permanent entering with four +1/+1 counters already on it.

3. **Doubling Season's interaction.** Doubling Season says, "If an effect would put one or more counters on a permanent you control, it puts twice that many of those counters on that permanent instead." Skullbriar entering the battlefield with counters is an effect putting counters on a permanent you control. Doubling Season ruling #2 explicitly states that Doubling Season affects permanents that enter with counters. Therefore, Doubling Season's replacement effect applies, and instead of putting four +1/+1 counters on Skullbriar, you put eight +1/+1 counters on it.

4. **Skullbriar ruling #2 does not prevent this.** Skullbriar ruling #2 says, "The counters that remain on Skullbriar as it changes zones aren't 'placed' on Skullbriar. Effects like Doubling Season's and Melira, Sylvok Outcast's won't affect those counters." This ruling means that Doubling Season does not double the counters *as they remain on Skullbriar during zone changes*. However, when Skullbriar actually *enters the battlefield*, the game is putting counters on a permanent you control as part of that event. This is a separate event from the counters "remaining" during a zone change; it is an effect putting counters on a permanent, which Doubling Season does affect. The ruling prevents Doubling Season from, for example, doubling the counters when Skullbriar moves from the graveyard to the command zone, but it does not prevent Doubling Season from applying to the event of Skullbriar entering the battlefield with those counters.

Thus, Skullbriar enters the battlefield with eight +1/+1 counters.

results.question: I cast [Final Fortune] to take an extra turn. During that extra turn I use [Sundial of the Infinite] to end the turn before the end step. Do I still lose the game?
results.text: No, you do not lose the game. Sundial of the Infinite's ability ends the turn, which skips the end step entirely. Final Fortune's delayed triggered ability triggers only at the beginning of that turn's end step, so it never gets a chance to trigger and you never lose the game.

results.question: I cast [Clone]. When and how do I choose what it copies, and can my opponent respond to that choice?
results.text:
You choose what Clone copies as it enters the battlefield, not while it is on the stack. This choice is made during the resolution of the Clone spell, as a replacement effect that modifies how Clone enters. Your opponent cannot respond to the choice itself, but they can respond to the Clone spell while it is on the stack, before you have made any choice.

Here's the step-by-step:
1. You cast Clone and it goes on the stack. At this point, you have not yet chosen what it will copy. Your opponent can respond to the Clone spell with instants or abilities.
2. When Clone resolves, it would normally enter the battlefield as a 0/0 creature. However, Clone's own ability creates a replacement effect: "You may have this creature enter as a copy of any creature on the battlefield." This effect modifies how Clone enters [707.5].
3. As Clone enters the battlefield, you apply that replacement effect and choose a creature already on the battlefield for Clone to copy. Clone then enters as a copy of that creature, acquiring its copiable values [707.2].
4. Because the choice is made as part of a replacement effect during the resolution of the spell, no player receives priority between the choice being made and Clone entering the battlefield. Your opponent cannot respond to the choice.

If you choose not to copy anything, Clone enters as a 0/0 Shapeshifter and will likely die immediately due to having 0 toughness [Clone ruling #5].

This answer assumes a two-player game. In a multiplayer game, the same timing applies—the choice is made as Clone enters, and no player can respond to the choice itself.

results.question: I activate my [Flooded Strand]'s ability, then activate [Gogo, Master of Mimicry] with X=2 to copy it twice. How many lands do I get from that one Flooded Strand?
results.text:
You get three lands total: the one from the original Flooded Strand ability plus two from the copies. Each copy resolves independently and searches for a Plains or Island, puts it onto the battlefield, then shuffles. The original Flooded Strand is sacrificed only once, as part of paying the cost of the original ability, and that sacrifice does not prevent the copies from resolving. The copies are put directly onto the stack by Gogo, Master of Mimicry's ability; they are not activated, so they do not require paying the sacrifice cost again.

Here's why: Gogo, Master of Mimicry's ability targets an activated ability on the stack (the Flooded Strand's fetch ability) and creates copies of it. According to rule 707.10b, a copy of an ability copies all decisions made for the original, including targets (none here) and the value of X (not applicable here), but not choices made on resolution. The copy is put onto the stack and is itself an ability. The original Flooded Strand's cost—tapping, paying 1 life, and sacrificing Flooded Strand—was already paid when the original ability was activated. The copies are not activated, so no additional costs are paid. Each copy resolves normally, performing the full effect: search for a Plains or Island, put it onto the battlefield, then shuffle. Since the original ability and both copies all resolve, you end up with three lands from that one Flooded Strand card.

Gogo, Master of Mimicry ruling #6 confirms that Gogo's ability creates additional instances of the targeted ability on the stack and does not cause any object to gain abilities. Gogo, Master of Mimicry ruling #9 confirms the source of each copy is the same as the original ability's source (the Flooded Strand), but that does not impose additional costs. Rule 707.10b explicitly states that a copy of an ability is not activated, so no costs are paid for the copies. The sacrifice of Flooded Strand is a cost of the original activation only; the copies exist independently on the stack and resolve even though the source permanent is no longer on the battlefield (the ability on the stack is independent of its source once activated).
